title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs. Ahmed Heakl, Martin Gubri, Salman Khan, Sangdoo Yun, Seong Joon Oh (Parameter Lab, MBZUAI, NAVER AI Lab, Tuebingen). Header: 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026'
id_read: arXiv 2510.12773v2 (18 May 2026), pdftotext of full PDF, 1312 lines. (First pass read v1 which said 'Under submission'; v2 confirms ICLR 2026.)
setup: Dense decoder LLMs: LLaMA-3.2-3B (Instruct, Base), LLaMA-3.1-8B (Instruct, Base), Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (no MoE). One NVIDIA A100 40GB for router training (4 h, 25 epochs, routers 11M params for 3B = 0.14%, 16.8M for 8B = 0.56%). Router = Linear-GELU-Linear per layer (width 128) reading windowed mean-pooled hidden states (W=8); labels from offline length-aware MCTS (50 simulations, 961k forward passes) on 4,000 ARC/DART-Math examples; labels skip 7.6%, repeat 2.3%. IMPORTANT (Sec 3.1): routers run ONCE per input sequence, so the skip/execute/repeat path is fixed per prompt, not decided per generated token. Baselines: vanilla model, LayerSkip, ShortGPT, MindSkip, FlexiDepth (numbers copied from FlexiDepth paper, LLaMA-3-8B). Eval: lm-eval-harness, greedy, max 2048 tokens. Wall-clock hardware for the 29.21 s / Table 7 numbers is not stated beyond the A100 used for training (assumed A100, not stated). Batch sizes 1..128 in Table 7 (LLaMA-3B-Instruct).

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'abstract/body inconsistent on layers saved (5 vs up to 11)'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: the 11 is a per-dataset DART figure (-10.96 LLaMA-8B-Instruct); abstract 5 is the mean; also MCTS labels save only 1.82 layers on average (Sec 4.2)

why: Assumption that breaks: (1) dense models and no expert reads, so skipping a layer saves compute not streamed bytes; (2) the skip is ~1% of layer applications and chosen once per prompt, so it cannot approach our 25-67% skip scenario; (3) the 15-27% wall-time gains are 10-25x larger than the 1-2% layer reduction and are not explained by the paper (undefined GPU timing setup), so they cannot be used as evidence for any byte-saving; (4) GPU, batch 1-128, A100; (5) routers are trained per model on 4k labels, retraining per MoE model needed. The skipped layers in a streamed-expert model would also skip that layer's expert reads, which the paper never studies.
quality_loss: In-domain (ARC/DART, trained on) +0.9..+3.2 points; out-of-domain mean -0.85 points over 8 benchmarks (Table 4), worst single tasks AGIEval -4.8 (Qwen3B), PIQA -3.7 (LLaMA3B), GPQA Diamond +2.6 (LLaMA3B). No perplexity reported.
ablation: Fig 5 (3B): router bottleneck dim, number of linear layers, number of pooling windows; focal loss vs weighted CE (+1.1 ARC, +1.8 DART); Table 6: routing from previous-layer hidden state (74.5/38.6) vs from embeddings H1 (70.9/30.0) vs vanilla (73.5/35.2). No ablation separating skip from repeat on accuracy or speed.
limitations: No dedicated Limitations section found (grep). Authors mention repeat only 2.3% of layers so batch sync cheap; 80-89% inter-sequence routing consensus (Table 8).
contradicts_our_findings: Partly contradicts a line in our D.md: 'ShortGPT/Dr.LLM remove or skip only 10-25% of layers ... our arithmetic gives 1.11-1.33x'. For Dr.LLM the true skip is ~1% of layer applications, so the matching claim does not hold for Dr.LLM (it holds only for ShortGPT-style 25% removal). Nothing in the paper contradicts our 1/kept arithmetic or the chance-level adjacent-layer Jaccard (different quantity).

why: Assumptions that break: (1) the speedup is draft-and-verify (lossless wrt the LayerSkip model) and needs a model pretrained/finetuned with the recipe, which no available MoE has; (2) the verify pass checks d=4-12 draft tokens at once, which in a sparse MoE touches up to d x 10 distinct experts per layer, so streamed bytes per verified token can rise, not fall (my inference; the paper has no MoE); (3) dense Llama only, GPU (CPU only for a 1.5B model); (4) early-exit alone is the only part that saves bytes and it destroys quality without verification (ROUGE-2 0.012 vs 0.079).
quality_loss: Self-speculative output is the same as the LayerSkip model's own greedy output (EM 82.9% at all E in Table 6). Cost is in the model: LayerSkip continual pretraining lowers last-layer accuracy (Llama3 8B MMLU 66.5 -> 60.5; Table 2); for Llama2 7B/13B it is small (Table 1, partly read). Early exit alone is lossy: TOPv2 EM 85.9 -> 79.4 at E=12, 62.9 at E=6.
ablation: Fig 12/appendix: layer-dropout schedule vs constant; Table 7: KV and exit-query cache reuse saves 9-20 ms/token on CPU; self-speculative vs early exit rows in Tables 3-6. No MoE ablation.
limitations: Sec 8: requires finetuning or pretraining; hyperparameters pmax, escale, R need tuning; learning rate must be raised for pretraining from scratch.
contradicts_our_findings: None. Does not conflict with our 1/kept arithmetic; it is a different mechanism and our trace tests cannot test it.

why: Evidence that layer-wise early exit potential is small in modern models (oracle skips 0.04-7% of layers within 5% loss) supports our caution about the 'run 16 of 48 layers' idea, including for MoE (Llama4-Scout 0.18-0.32%, OSS-20B 4.5-7.3%). Breaks: early exit (stop at layer l, drop the tail) is not the same as per-sequence or per-token skipping of arbitrary middle layers; no MoE-specific bytes analysis; hidden-state cosine to the final layer, not task quality; 100 prompts per task; hardware not reported.
quality_loss: Oracle (cheating) exit: MMLU -0.02 to -0.05, GSM8K -0.03 to -0.04 accuracy at the stated tiny skip fractions; thresholds chosen to keep the loss at most 5%. Practical confidence-based exits are worse (paper text: 'fails to achieve a balance').

limitations: Limitations section: only methods with little/no training considered (fine-tuned exits or auxiliary heads could do better); training recipes of open models unknown.
contradicts_our_findings: None numerically. It gives a second weak signal that MoE models are not more skippable than dense; our adjacent-layer expert Jaccard (chance level) is a different quantity and neither contradicts nor supports this.

Models: DeepSeek-V2-Lite ('64x2.4B'), Switch-128x0.2B, NLLB-128x0.4B, Arctic-128x4B, Mixtral-8x7B. 290 tasks from BIGBench, FLAN, MMLU; batch size 1; prompt 512, decode 32; TPOT averaged. title: QMoE: Practical Sub-1-Bit Compression of Trillion-Parameter Models. Elias Frantar, Dan Alistarh (IST Austria)
id_read: arXiv 2310.16795v1 (25 Oct 2023), full PDF text, 898 lines. Venue not printed (MLSys 2024 from memory).
setup: Data-dependent (GPTQ-style) quantization of SwitchTransformer base128, large128, c2048 (1.6T params, 2048 experts, top-1, T5 encoder-decoder, MLM pretraining) to 2-bit and ternary, then a custom dictionary/entropy code (pairs of ternary values, fixed 16-bit-ish dictionary in GPU L2) with fused GPU decode+matvec kernels. Compression: one A6000 48GB, under a day (Table 8: 20.8 h for c2048 at 20K/320K calibration samples), few hundred GB CPU RAM. Inference: 4x A6000 or 8x RTX 3090, HuggingFace, offloading to CPU memory for sparse layers in compression stage. Metrics: C4 validation loss (128 samples), plus Arxiv/Github/StackExchange/Wikipedia loss; no zero-shot accuracy. Baselines: BF16, RTN (identity Hessian).

numbers.baseline: BF16 estimate obtained by pointing all experts of a layer at the same weight memory ('highly optimistic', lower bound)

numbers.value: up to 35% faster than BF16 on some shapes (smallest matrix <0.02 ms)

catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: post-training, data-dependent quantization with calibration data

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: dictionary coding on ternary weights with GPU decode kernels
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: Sec 4
baseline is an estimated lower bound, not a run

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'mixtral-offloading authors report sub-1-bit QMoE gave too much perplexity loss on Mixtral'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: that claim is about another paper; not in QMoE text (from first pass only)

why: Assumptions that break: 0.8 bits exists only because 88.6% of ternary-rounded weights are zero (natural sparsity grows with expert count: 85.7% at 128 experts, 88.6% at 2048), which is a property of Switch c2048's tiny, redundant experts; ternary loss already grows from +6.8% (2048 experts) to +15% (128 experts); the T5 encoder-decoder MLM model is not a decoder LLM with 512 experts top-10; custom GPU kernel (GPU L2-resident dictionary); no CPU decoder; no downstream accuracy. A 512-expert top-10 decoder sits between the 128 and 2048 expert Switch points, nearer the lossy end.
quality_loss: C4 validation loss only: +6.8% (c2048 ternary), +1.7% (2-bit), +9% (large128), +15% (base128); RTN ternary +82% on c2048. No benchmark accuracy.
ablation: Tables 2-3: special-token masking (base128 ternary 2.16 -> 1.99), activation reordering and sequential execution (heuristics, ineffective). Calibration sample count (Table 5 0.5x/1x/2x). No ablation of dictionary vs plain ternary packing on loss.
limitations: Sec 7: only SwitchTransformers evaluated, bespoke frameworks hinder other MoEs; compressed-model finetuning unexplored.
contradicts_our_findings: None. Consistent with our 'not comparable, not tested' status; adds that gains scale with expert count in the paper's own data (ternary loss grows as experts shrink), a useful prior for 512 experts.

title: Mixture of Quantized Experts (MoQE): Complementary Effect of Low-bit Quantization and Robustness. Young Jin Kim, Raffy Fahim, Hany Hassan Awadalla (Microsoft)
id_read: arXiv 2310.02410v1 (3 Oct 2023), full PDF text, 623 lines. Footer: 'Preprint. Under review.'
setup: Weight-only linear (channel-wise) quantization of expert FFN weights only (rest fp16). Multilingual machine-translation Transformer, 5.3B-parameter MoE with 32 experts, top-1 gating, MoE every other layer, vs FLOPs-equivalent dense model; 200,000 updates on internal 6-language data (Table 2, 6, 7) and WMT-10 public (Table 5). Metric BLEU (sacrebleu). Hardware: single NVIDIA A100, CUDA 11.6. Throughput batch size 24 sentences (Table 1). No kernel below 4 bit. 2-bit needs QAT.

numbers.ratio: int2 QAT is -0.45 BLEU (-0.97%) vs MoE fp16 and +0.84 BLEU vs dense fp16; size 0.20x = 79.6% reduction

catalog_numbers_correct.claim: First-pass: 'headline int2 uses QAT; catalog omits it'
catalog_numbers_correct.true_value: abstract and Sec 3.1

why: Assumptions that break: machine-translation encoder-decoder with 32 small experts, top-1; 5.3B params; not an LLM; BLEU not a language-model quality measure; headline 2-bit needs QAT (retraining); no optimized kernel below 4 bit, speedup (1.24x) is 4-bit on A100 at batch 24. Qualitative message (experts have fewer outliers, so post-training 3-bit is nearly free and 2-bit costs 3-12% BLEU where dense collapses) is the only transferable part; it is a different architecture from a 512-expert top-10 decoder.
quality_loss: Post-training: 3-bit -0.4..-1.2% BLEU; 2-bit -3..-12% BLEU (depending on dataset). With QAT 2-bit: -0.97% vs fp16 MoE (45.90 vs 46.35).
ablation: Fig 2 component sensitivity (experts vs dense FFN vs attention), Fig 4 linear vs log quantization, Fig 5 channel-wise vs matrix-wise scaling, Fig 6 which dense layers; no cache or layout ablation.
limitations: Sec 4: no optimized implementation below 4 bits; 2-bit requires QAT; hybrid precision across layers not explored.
contradicts_our_findings: None. Our closed-form byte-lever (2.0 bpw: 1.75x serial / 1.09x overlap at 8 GB) is not tested by this paper. Correction to the first pass: the 'quantization hurts a lot post-training' impression came from a percent-vs-BLEU unit error; the real PTQ 2-bit damage is 3-12% BLEU relative.
